newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia issues latest mining contracts.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia issues latest mining contracts.

text.p: Indonesia on Monday formally allowed dozens of companies to explore for and mine minerals across the archipelago even as the cloud of the controversial Busang gold discovery hung over its mining sector.

Mines and Energy Minister Ida Bagus Sudjana witnessed the signing of 65 contracts of work (COWs) by executives of mining companies from Canada, the United States, Australia, South Africa, Netherlands, Papua New Guinea and South Korea.
They will be exploring for and possibly mining minerals ranging from gold to copper and diamonds from the northern tip of Sumatra Island to the far reaches of Irian Jaya province.
The contracts were approved by parliament last July but their issuance had been held up by the controversy surrounding the Busang property in Indonesia's East Kalimantan province.

"This ceremony is very important...and timely because it makes a very clear statement to the world about the promising future of the mining industry in Indonesia," Robert Chase, president and chief executive officer of South Pacific Resources Corp, told the gathering.

Speaking on behalf of the foreign companies granted contracts, he said foreign companies were demonstrating their continued commitment to the exploration and development of the country's rich mineral deposits by signing the contracts.

"I think Indonesia continues to be one of the most prospective places in the world for international investment in the mining sector today, regardless of what happens with Busang," he later told Reuters.
Chase said junior mining companies had already felt the impact of Busang and that they were looking forward to getting on with their business once the controversy was clarified.
Canadian consulting company Strathcona Mineral Services Ltd was carrying out an independent audit of the gold content at the Busang property and the results were expected later this week.

Bre-X stunned the world last month when it said there was a strong possibility the potential gold resources on the Busang property might have been overstated. It had previously estimated that Busang contained some 70.95 million ounces of gold worth $25 billion, making it the biggest find this century.
Bre-X owns 45-percent of the Busang property, Freeport McMoRan Copper and Gold Inc has 15 percent and Indonesian interests the remaining 40 percent.
Sudjana said he was unaware of any intentions by Freeport to pull out of the project as reported last week by the local Harian Ekonomi Neraca newspaper.
"They (Freeport) have not reported," he told reporters, adding that the government has not been informed of the results of Strathcona's independent audit of Busang.
The newspaper said the firm was planning to officially withdraw before results of an inedependent audit to determine the gold content in Busang were announced.
Freeport said in a statement in late March that it would elect to participate in the development of the project only if developing the find was economically feasible.
He also said two applications for COWs by Bre-X to further explore and develop Busang had yet to be approved, adding that they were still "at the desk" of the ministry director-general.
John Loney, president-director of PT Placer Emas Indonesia, a unit of Placer Dome of Canada, said the company saw Indonesia as being very attractive for gold mining.

"From what we know, the government has always honoured the contract of work, so we see that as a very good system. From a geological point of view we see Indonesia as very prospective for gold," he told Reuters after signing a COW for gold exploration in South Kalimantan on Borneo Island.
He said major mining companies such as Placer Dome which relied on internal cash flow for exploration, would not be hit by the Busang controversy.
